rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Quraysh became overbearing, the Prophet prayed that God intensify hardship on Muḍar and afflict them with years like Joseph’s; Mecca then lacked water and vegetation.
rows.anchor: أن قريشا لما طغت، دعا عليها رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mecca was barren, but God blessed nearby places such as al-Ṭāʾif and caused varieties of fruit to grow there.
rows.anchor: وكانت مكة إذ ذاك قفرا، لا ماء بها ولا نبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says God sent Gabriel to uproot Palestine, or a region of Jordan, circle it around the Kaaba seven times, and set it down in the valley; this is offered as the origin of al-Ṭāʾif’s name.
rows.anchor: وروي أن الله تعالى لما دعاه إبراهيم، أمر جبريل فاقتلع فلسطين

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some derive al-Ṭāʾif’s name from the circling described in the report; an unattributed couplet praises places that circumambulate the sanctuary.
rows.anchor: فسميت الطائف بسبب ذلك الطواف، وقال بعضهم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith in God entails belief in the necessary Creator and His fitting attributes; faith in the Last Day entails reward and punishment, accountability, and thus the prophets and their message, so the two beliefs encompass required faith.
rows.anchor: لأن في الإيمان بالله إيمانا بالصانع الواجب الوجود، وبما يليق به تعالى من الصفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s prayer for the people of the House covers everyone called its people, not only his descendants, although the wording about provision appears restricted to descendants by its pronoun.
rows.anchor: ودعاء إبراهيم لأهل البيت يعم من يطلق عليه هذا الاسم، ولا يختص ذلك بذريته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording may comprise two requests, since the provision request appears confined to Abraham’s descendants by the pronoun referring back to his statement that he settled some of them there.
rows.anchor: فيحتمل أن يكونا سؤالين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition min is partitive: the people were given only some of the fruits.
rows.anchor: ومن: في قوله: من الثمرات للتبعيض، لأنهم لم يرزقوا إلا بعض الثمرات.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative takes min as explanatory of kind and construes it as a partitive or inclusive apposition to أهله; specifying the subset after the general term repeats it for emphasis.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هي لبيان الجنس، ومن بدل من أهله، بدل بعض من كل، أو بدل اشتمال

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ initially raises man as a subject and rejects an accusative conditional analysis because, he says, a conditional particle cannot be governed by its answer; Abū Ḥayyān rejects that rationale.
rows.anchor: ثم إنه قد ناقض أبو البقاء في تجويزه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says the subject analysis is unnecessary: the enjoyment and eventual arrival in Hell are consequences deserved for unbelief, and the same author allows a conditional man with a fāʾ answer elsewhere.
rows.anchor: لأن التمتع القليل والصيرورة إلى النار مستحقان بالكفر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause is eloquent and coherent without positing an extra fāʾ, an omitted predicate, or an omitted conditional answer; Abū Ḥayyān criticizes such needless remote estimates in Qurʾānic parsing.
rows.anchor: وأما تقدير زيادة الفاء، وإضمار الخبر، وإضمار جواب الشرط، إذا جعلنا من شرطية، فلا حاجة إلى ذلك

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī coordinates man kafara with man āmana, as he also coordinates min dhurriyatī with the pronoun in jaʿiluka; Abū Ḥayyān rejects the first coordination because it would make Abraham command provision for unbelievers and conflict with the ensuing divine report.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ومن كفر: عطف على من آمن، كما عطف ومن ذريتي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says Abraham singled out believers because leadership is a trust for those who counsel well, whereas provision can be a divine test or a means of establishing proof; he reads the meaning as providing for unbelievers and then granting brief enjoyment.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت: لم خص إبراهيم المؤمنين حتى رد عليه؟ قلت: قاس الرزق على الإمامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects the premise that God answered a request to provide for believers: the verse reports the unbeliever’s brief enjoyment and final arrival in Hell, and does not rebuke Abraham or compare provision with leadership.
rows.anchor: وليس هنا قياس الرزق على الإمامة، ولا تعريف الفرق بينهما، كما زعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Matāʿ is anything used for benefit; here tamtīʿ or imtāʿ can mean prolonging life, facilitating benefits, supplying provisions, or giving the nonlasting enjoyment of worldly life. The hamza form makes someone an owner of such provision.
rows.anchor: وفسر هنا التمتيع والإمتاع بالإبقاء، أو بتيسير المنافع، ومنه متاع الحياة الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled verb mataʿ likewise means making someone possess what its root denotes, as in ʿadaltuhu; doubling does not itself indicate abundance and therefore does not conflict with the description ‘little.’
rows.anchor: وليس التضعيف في متع يقتضي التكثير، فينافي ظاهر ذلك القلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qalīlan can modify an omitted time expression, an omitted verbal noun according to most grammarians, or serve as a circumstantial accusative from the implicit verbal noun according to Sībawayh.
rows.anchor: وانتصاب قليلا على أنه صفة لظرف محذوف، أي زمانا قليلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators explain the enjoyment as brief because death comes, or Muḥammad appears and kills or expels them if they persist in unbelief; others mean worldly luxury, delayed punishment, provision, or mere survival.
rows.anchor: إما لحلول الأجل، وإما بظهور محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم فيقتله، أو يخرجه عن هذا البلد

rows.speaker: يحيى بن وثاب
rows.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb reads the hamza in ثم إضطره with kasra.
rows.anchor: وقراءة يحيى بن وثاب: ثم إضطره بكسر الهمزة.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes the kasra in the initial hamza to Qurashī usage, citing lā ikhālu; Abū Ḥayyān notes that this conflicts with grammarians’ general account of Hijazi vowel patterns, unless Quraysh uniquely had this form.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية، على لغة قريش، في قولهم: لا إخال

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin reads ثم أطره, assimilating ḍād into ṭāʾ; al-Zamakhsharī calls the dialect reprehensible because he says ḍād assimilates to neighboring letters but is not assimilated.
rows.anchor: وقراءة ابن محيصن: ثم أطره، بإدغام الضاد في الطاء.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls assimilation of ḍād into ṭāʾ a reprehensible dialect, but Abū Ḥayyān rejects the categorical prohibition: Sībawayh records Arabs saying muṭjaʿ for muḍṭajaʿ and explains why ḍād differs acoustically from ṣād.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: هي لغة مرذولة، لأن الضاد من الحروف الخمسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports of ḍād assimilating into dhāl in الأرض ذلولا and shīn in بعض شأنهم and الأرض شيئا are called weak; a report of shīn into sīn in إلى ذي العرش سبيلا is attributed to Abū ʿAmr but rejected by Basrans.
rows.anchor: وأما الشين فأدغمت في السين. روي عن أبي عمرو ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī’s reading assimilates fāʾ into bāʾ in إن نشأ نخسف بهم; although Khalīl and Sībawayh reject rāʾ into lām or nūn, Yaʿqūb, Abū ʿAmr, al-Kisāʾī, al-Farrāʾ, and al-Ruʾāsī permit rāʾ into lām on Arab authority, disproving consensus against such assimilation.
rows.anchor: وأما الراء، فذهب الخليل وسيبويه وأصحابه إلى أنه لا يجوز إدغام الراء في اللام

rows.speaker: ابن أبي حبيب
rows.claim: Ibn Abī Ḥabīb reads the ṭāʾ with ḍamma, analogically matching it to the rāʾ’s vowel; Abū Ḥayyān calls this anomalous.
rows.anchor: وقراءة ابن أبي حبيب: بضم الطاء، توجيهها أنه أتبع حركة الطاء لحركة الراء، وهو شاذ.

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: The reading attributed to Ubay with nūn in both verbs conflicts with the consonantal muṣḥaf and is therefore anomalous.
rows.anchor: وأما قراءة أبي بالنون فيهما، فهي مخالفة لرسم المصحف، فهي شاذة.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reads the clause as an imperative, repeating qāla either for emphasis or to make two separate prayers, one for believers and one against unbelievers, rather than placing both under one governing verb.
rows.anchor: وقراءة ابن عباس بصيغة الأمر يكون تكرير قال على سبيل التوكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iḍṭirār here means being compelled into the punishment with no escape when confined, not preferring or choosing entry into Hell.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الاضطرار هنا هو أنه يلجأ ويلز إلى العذاب، بحيث لا يجد محيصا عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional implication is set aside: the verse does not imply that only unbelievers can enter Hell, since sinful believers may enter it too.
rows.anchor: ومفهوم الشرط هنا ملغى، إذ قد يدخل النار بعض العصاة من المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condemned object is omitted as understood: al-nār if al-maṣīr means a place, or its becoming a destination in punishment if it is a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وبئس المصير المخصوص بالذم محذوف لفهم المعنى، أي وبئس المصير النار

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says his grammatical school rejects taking min as explanatory in the cited phrase and instead reinterprets examples that appear to support that analysis.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم لنا أن كون من للتبيين يأباه أصحابنا ويتأولون ما فهم من ظاهره ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Umma here means a community or a generation.
rows.anchor: وتقدم شرح الأمة، والمراد به هنا: الجماعة، أو الجيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min dhurriyyatinā is the first object of ijʿal, with jaʿl meaning to make or transform: make people from our descendants a community devoted to You; reading the omitted verb as ‘create’ is grammatically unavailable under the coordination.
rows.anchor: لأن الجعل هنا بمعنى التصيير، فالمعنى: واجعل ناسا من ذريتنا أمة مسلمة لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted ‘create’ cannot be supplied in coordination: a coordinated word shares the first verb’s non-creative sense, and an omitted coordinated clause must be licensed by the expressed wording, as illustrated by the different senses of God’s and the angels’ ṣalāt.
rows.anchor: وإن كان من باب عطف الجمل، فلا يحذف إلا ما دل عليه المنطوق

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ instead makes umma the first object, min dhurriyyatinā a circumstantial phrase, and muslimatan the second object; Abū Ḥayyān says separating the coordinated noun from its conjunction by a circumstantial phrase is more strained than separation by an adverb and should be confined to poetic necessity.
rows.anchor: وأجاز أبو البقاء أن يكون المفعول الأول أمة، ومن ذريتنا حال

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda explains manāsik as the landmarks or rites of the pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: وأرنا مناسكنا: قال قتادة: معالم الحج.

rows.speaker: عطاء وابن جريج
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ and Ibn Jurayj explain manāsik as the slaughter places, meaning the locations for sacrifice.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء وابن جريج: مذابحنا، أي مواضع الذبح.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view understands manāsik broadly as every act of worship by which God is worshipped.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كل عبادة يتعبد بها الله تعالى.

rows.speaker: تاج القراء الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmānī distinguishes manāsik as either the varied rites of Hajj or the places where its ordinances are observed.
rows.anchor: وقال تاج القراء الكرماني: إن كان المراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the rites of Hajj, including ṭawāf, saʿy, standing, and prayer, manāsik is a plural of the verbal noun due to their variety; if the stations such as Minā, ʿArafa, and Muzdalifa are intended, it is a plural of the place noun.
rows.anchor: أعمال الحج، وما يفعل في المواقف، كالطواف، والسعي، والوقوف، والصلاة

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report from ʿAlī says that after Abraham finished building the House and made this prayer, God sent Gabriel, who performed the pilgrimage with him.
rows.anchor: وروي عن علي أن إبراهيم لما فرغ من بناء البيت ودعا بهذه الدعوة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads وأرهم مناسكهم, returning the pronoun to Abraham’s descendants.
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة ابن مسعود: وأرهم مناسكهم، أعاد الضمير على الذرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān takes arinā as causative of visual seeing: the base verb takes one object and the hamza makes it take two, matching the construction; if it were ordinary cognitive seeing, the causative would require three.
rows.anchor: فإذا دخلت عليها همزة النقل، تعدت إلى ثلاثة، وليس هنا إلا اثنان

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī takes the verb as cognitive seeing meaning ‘know,’ with one object before causativization and two after it; Abū Ḥayyān says this requires attestation in Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: وقد جعلها الزمخشري من رؤية القلب، وشرحها بقوله: عرف

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports both visual and cognitive analyses and favors visual seeing, while addressing the three-object objection by claiming causative cognitive raʾā can occur with two; Abū Ḥayyān says the cited poetic example does not establish that claim.
rows.anchor: وحكى ابن عطية عن طائفة أنها من رؤية البصر، وعن طائفة أنها من رؤية القلب

rows.speaker: الكميت
rows.claim: The cited anonymous line and al-Kumayt’s verse illustrate cognitive raʾā taking two objects, which is why adding the causative hamza would ordinarily yield three.
rows.anchor:
وقال الكميت:
بأي كتاب أم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse of Ibn Yaʿfar cited by Ibn ʿAṭiyya does not prove cognitive raʾā with one object: ‘show me a fine horse’ is visibly perceptible, especially given the horse’s dying of starvation; Abū Ḥayyān requires an actual linguistic attestation.
rows.anchor: بل الظاهر أنها بصرية، والمعنى على أبصريني جوادا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān invokes Ibn Mālik’s comprehensive account of verbs taking two objects: its exclusions conflict with treating raʾā here as cognitive ‘know,’ so that usage needs evidence.
rows.anchor: وقد قال ابن مالك، وهو حاشد لغة، وحافظ نوادر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposal that arinā simultaneously means both visual and cognitive seeing is weak: it combines literal with metaphorical meaning or gives a shared word multiple senses at once, which Abū Ḥayyān disallows.
rows.anchor: وهذا ضعيف، لأن فيه الجمع بين الحقيقة والمجاز

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads arinā and five instances of arinī with sukūn on the rāʾ; Abū ʿAmr is reported with sukūn and ikhtilās as well as full articulation, while Abū ʿĀmir and Abū Bakr use sukūn in the two occurrences of arinā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير: وأرنا، وأرني خمسة بإسكان الراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Full articulation is the underlying form, ikhtilās is elegant and well known, and sukūn analogizes the separate pronoun-like form to a connected one; the reading is not an invalid deletion of the kasra.
rows.anchor: فالإشباع هو الأصل، والاختلاس حسن مشهور في العربية، والإسكان تشبيه للمنفصل بالمتصل

rows.speaker: الفارسي
rows.claim: Al-Fārisī rejects the objection that sukūn wrongly removes the kasra that once signaled the deleted hamza: the derivational base is no longer active, and Arabic also drops a moved vowel before assimilation, as in lakinnā huwa Allāhu rabbī.
rows.anchor: وقال الفارسي: ما قاله هذا القائل ليس بشيء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says sukūn on the rāʾ is explicitly attested from Arabs in a poetic line.
rows.anchor: وأيضا فقد سمع الإسكان في هذا الحرف نصا عن العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān adds that sukūn is mutawātir, so denying the reading is untenable.
rows.anchor: وأيضا فهي قراءة متواترة، فإنكارها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators give seven conflicting reports on how Abraham and Ishmael performed the rites and list prophets who made pilgrimage or died in Mecca; the verse says none of this, so Abū Ḥayyān omits the accounts.
rows.anchor: وذكر المفسرون في كيفية تأدية إبراهيم وإسماعيل هذه المناسك، أقوالا سبعة مضطربة النقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repentance for ordinary Muslims entails remorse, abandoning sin, resolve not to return, and restoring wronged rights if possible or intending to do so if not; the spiritual elite repent of disliked thoughts and imperfect worship, while the elite of the elite seek higher ranks.
rows.anchor: فتوبة سائر المسلمين الندم بالقلب، والرجوع عن الذنب، والعزم على عدم العود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Abraham and Ishmael ask repentance for themselves, it could mean the highest level of seeking advancement, or a prayer to remain steadfast as in ‘make us Muslims’; if the pronoun includes descendants, the request can concern those among them who need repentance.
rows.anchor: فيحتمل أن تكون التوبة هنا من هذا القسم الأخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not prove that prophets sinned, contrary to the argument that repentance presupposes a prior sin: the pronoun may concern sinful descendants, a possibility supported by Abraham’s prayer about those of his offspring who disobey.
rows.anchor: ولا تدل هذه الآية على جواز وقوع الذنب من الأنبياء عليهم الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: The reading attributed to ʿAbd Allāh has أرهم مناسكهم; Abū Ḥayyān also allows the written form to omit an understood possessive, meaning ‘show us our descendants’ rites,’ by analogy with addressing descendants while referring to their ancestor’s creation.
rows.anchor: وقراءة عبد الله، وأرهم مناسكهم، وتب عليهم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the prayer may ask forgiveness for minor lapses by the two patriarchs, or may seek repentance for their descendants; Abū Ḥayyān notes that the first reflects the Muʿtazilī allowance of minor prophetic sins.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وتب علينا ما فرط منا من الصغائر، أو استتابا لذريتهما.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers that the patriarchs modeled seeking repentance at the site after completing the rites and building the House; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this as a very remote departure from the prayer’s apparent meaning.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وقد ذكر قولي التثبيت، أو كون ذلك دعاء للذرية

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya states a consensus that prophets are protected in conveying revelation, from major sins, and from reprehensible minor sins, with disagreement about other minor sins.
rows.anchor: وأجمعت الأمة على عصمة الأنبياء في معنى التبليغ، ومن الكبائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anta may be a separating pronoun, an emphatic pronoun, or a subject; tawwāb and raḥīm suit the prayers for submission, a faithful community, guidance in the rites, and repentance.
rows.anchor: يجوز في أنت: الفصل والتأكيد والابتداء، وهاتان الصفتان مناسبتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repentance precedes mercy because it echoes the immediately preceding request; mercy follows because it is broader and includes repentance, while raḥīm provides the appropriate verse ending amid the surrounding paired divine attributes.
rows.anchor: وناسب تقديم ذكر التوبة على الرحمة، لمجاورة الدعاء الأخير في قوله: وتب علينا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After prayers for Mecca’s security, its people’s provision, and a submissive community from Abraham’s descendants, the prayer concludes by asking for Muḥammad’s mission, which secures their worldly and otherworldly happiness through safety, abundance, and guidance.
rows.anchor: لما دعا ربه بالأمن لمكة، وبالرزق لأهلها، وبأن يجعل من ذريته أمة مسلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baʿth here means sending or commissioning as a messenger, as in the earlier explanation of the root in the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم معنى البعث في قوله: ثم بعثناكم، والمراد هنا: الإرسال إليهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in fīhim may refer to Abraham’s descendants, the submissive community, or the people of Mecca; the last is supported by the description of a messenger among the unlettered. The messenger is undisputedly Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: والضمير في فيهم يحتمل أن يعود على الذرية، ويحتمل أن يعود على أمة مسلمة

rows.speaker: محمد
rows.claim: A sound report has Muḥammad say, ‘I am the invocation of my father Abraham’; Abū Ḥayyān adds that God sent no one to Mecca and its surroundings except him.
rows.anchor:
ولا خلاف أنه رسول الله محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم، وصح عنه
أنه قال: «أنا دعوة أبي إبراهيم»

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubay reads وابعث فيهم في آخرهم, specifying their latter members.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي: وابعث فيهم في آخرهم، قال ابن عباس:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says all prophets were from the Children of Israel except ten, whom he names: Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Shuʿayb, Lūṭ, Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, and Muḥammad (the excerpt’s count and list are as reported).
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: كل الأنبياء من بني إسرائيل إلا عشرة: نوح، وهود، وصالح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Minhum is an adjective of rasūlan: the messenger is from the people, not outsiders, so they know his face, lineage, upbringing, truthfulness, and trustworthiness; an insider is more compassionate and more readily accepted and honored.
rows.anchor: ومنهم في موضع الصفة لرسولا، أي كائنا منهم لا من غيرهم

rows.speaker: الشيعة
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī reports the Shīʿa position that prophets cannot commit any sin, small or great, intentionally, accidentally, or by mistaken interpretation; he also notes agreement that they cannot disbelieve, alter the message, or err in legal judgment.
rows.anchor: قالت الشيعة، لا يجوز أن يقع

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī’s own position is that prophets never sin deliberately, whether greatly or slightly, but may err inadvertently if they recognize it immediately and tell others it was inadvertent.
rows.anchor: ثم قال الذي يقول به إنه لا يقع منهم ذنب على سبيل القصد، لا كبير ولا صغير
